summary: This document explains how IPv4 and IPv6 coexistence combined with poor IPv6 support in VPN products can make traffic that should go through an encrypted tunnel leak out unprotected on the local network. It discusses the problem and mitigations.

plainLanguage.summary: A VPN creates a protected tunnel for traffic, but many VPN programs protect only IPv4. On a computer that also speaks IPv6, some traffic takes the unprotected path instead, and can be read on the local network. RFC 7359 describes how that happens, how an attacker can make it happen, and how to stop it.

questions: why does my vpn leak ipv6 traffic
why does a vpn leak ipv6 traffic
what is a dual stack host
how to stop vpn ipv6 leak
subtitle: When a VPN guards IPv4 only, the IPv6 half of a dual-stack host can send traffic in the clear.

tldr.problem: Many VPN products handle IPv4 alone while the hosts running them are dual-stack, so traffic sent over IPv6 never enters the encrypted tunnel and leaves in the clear on the local network.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC explains how DNS records for both address families let a host pick IPv6, how an IPv6-unaware VPN client then leaves that traffic unprotected, how an attacker can force the situation with forged Router Advertisements, and what mitigations exist.
tldr.outcome: The proper fix is VPN software that handles IPv6; the temporary workaround is disabling IPv6 on every interface. An IESG Note printed with the RFC disputes the document's framing.

facts.label: DNS records involved
facts.value: A for IPv4 and AAAA for IPv6

facts.label: Temporary workaround
facts.value: Disable IPv6 on all network interfaces

today: RFC 7359 is an Informational RFC from August 2014, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It carries an IESG Note that disputes the document's framing of the problem as specific to IPv6-unaware VPN software.

sections.title: The Assumption and the Problem
sections.content:
People commonly use VPN software on public, possibly rogue local networks. They do so both to reach remote resources and to protect their traffic from attackers on the same local network, and that second reason is this document's subject. It is sometimes assumed that a VPN tunnel makes otherwise insecure protocols acceptable, because the tunnel provides data integrity and confidentiality for everything sent over it.

RFC 7359 shows that under certain circumstances some traffic may not be mapped onto the tunnel at all and so may be sent in the clear on the local network. The root of the trouble: many VPN products support only IPv4, securing IPv4 traffic while doing nothing for IPv6 traffic, yet the hosts they run on are typically dual-stacked, supporting and enabling both protocols by default. When such a host has IPv6 connectivity and uses an IPv6-unaware VPN client on a dual-stack network, traffic meant for the tunnel can leak out of it and reach the final destination without any VPN protection, either by accident or through a deliberate attack.

The issue is specific to VPN solutions that route Layer 3 traffic, so it applies to IPsec-based VPN tunnels and SSL/TLS VPN tunnels. The document excludes SSL/TLS VPN portals, which are application-specific front-ends that wrap a protocol such as HTTP and let all other traffic take the direct route.
sections.plainLanguage: People trust a VPN to protect everything they send, but the VPN may protect only one of the two ways a modern computer can talk to the Internet. The other way bypasses the tunnel and carries data openly.

sections.title: How IPv4 and IPv6 Coexist
sections.content:
IPv6 is not backwards-compatible with IPv4, but the Domain Name System (DNS) glues the two together. A site that supports both, such as www.example.com, has both A resource records and AAAA resource records under its name. Each A record holds one IPv4 address and each AAAA record one IPv6 address, and there may be several of each.

A dual-stacked client application can ask for both record types and use any of the addresses it receives. Which family it prefers, and which specific address it picks, varies between implementations, and many implementations prefer IPv6 addresses over IPv4 ones. RFC 6724 defines an algorithm for choosing among a list of IPv6 and IPv4 addresses, and RFC 6555 describes an approach that avoids connection-establishment delays while making that choice.

The practical consequence is simple: the A and AAAA records a name server returns usually decide which protocol a host uses to reach another system.
sections.plainLanguage: A name in the phone book can have two kinds of number, one for each version of the Internet Protocol. The computer asks for both and often picks the newer kind, so the phone book, not the VPN, decides which path the traffic takes.

sections.title: Where the Traffic Leaks Out
sections.content:
Many VPN tunnel implementations do not support IPv6, or worse, ignore it entirely. After a tunnel is established, the client software typically secures IPv4 by inserting an IPv4 default route, which sends all IPv4 traffic over the tunnel instead of to the local router. Packets addressed to an IPv6 address get nothing: the VPN software never touches them, so they leave in the clear through the local IPv6 router.

The deeper reason, in the RFC's words, is that on a dual-stacked system you cannot secure communication with another system without securing both protocols. As long as one protocol's traffic is unsecured, leakage is possible.

In the legitimate scenario this is an accident. A dual-stacked host running IPv4-only VPN software connects to a dual-stack network. An application looks up both record types for a dual-stacked destination, and one possible outcome is that the host uses IPv6. That traffic then gets neither integrity nor confidentiality protection from the source host to the final destination, exposing traffic that was assumed to be secured. The RFC also notes the split-tunnel case, where only part of the traffic is routed through the VPN and the rest takes a direct path by design.
sections.plainLanguage: The VPN program rewrites the routing so IPv4 goes into the tunnel, but it leaves IPv6 alone. Packets addressed the IPv6 way simply go out the normal door, unencrypted, even though the user believes they are protected.

sections.title: Deliberate Leakage Attacks
sections.content:
A local attacker can deliberately switch on IPv6 connectivity on the victim host by sending forged ICMPv6 Router Advertisement messages, as defined in RFC 4861. Standard software such as rtadvd or packet-crafting tools such as the SI6 IPv6 Toolkit and THC's IPv6 Attack Toolkit can produce such packets. Once IPv6 connectivity exists, communications with dual-stacked systems can leak as described.

That attack only bites when the destination is dual-stacked. To reach any destination, an attacker can instead advertise himself as the local recursive DNS server, by sending forged Router Advertisements carrying the Recursive DNS Server (RDNSS) option of RFC 6106, and then spoof DNS answers to insert himself as a man in the middle and intercept the traffic. The RFC notes that some systems prefer IPv6-based recursive DNS servers over IPv4-based ones, so the attacker's server can beat the legitimate one advertised by the VPN server.

The document's own security considerations restate the whole issue: traffic meant to travel over a VPN tunnel can leak out of it and appear in the clear on the local network, as a result of employing IPv6-unaware VPN client software on dual-stacked hosts.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone sharing your network can send a fake announcement that turns on IPv6, or pose as the name server, so your traffic leaves through the unprotected path where they can watch it.

sections.title: Mitigations
sections.content:
The RFC reports that at the time of writing a large number of VPN implementations had not addressed leakage; most simply ignore IPv6, so IPv6 traffic leaks. Some handle IPv6 but not properly: they may stop the accidental leaks on a legitimate dual-stack network yet fail against the routes an attacker can inject, such as ICMPv6 Router Advertisements carrying Prefix Information Options or Route Information Options (RFC 4191), and ICMPv6 Redirect messages.

For a client configured to send all IPv4 traffic through the VPN, the RFC gives two rules. If IPv6 is not supported in the VPN software, disable IPv6 support on all network interfaces, which leaves applications with no option but IPv4; the RFC stresses this is only a temporary workaround. If IPv6 is supported, make sure all IPv6 traffic is also sent through the VPN, which means handling every route-injection vector properly, and that may prove nontrivial.

For split-tunnel mode the rules mirror those: an IPv6-unaware client should disable IPv6 on all interfaces, and if the client is IPv6 aware, administrators must ensure the correct corresponding sets of IPv4 and IPv6 networks are routed into the tunnel.

A network can protect its local hosts with First-Hop Security such as Router Advertisement Guard (RFC 6105) and DHCPv6-Shield, but a host cannot rely on that on an open network such as a cybercafe, and popular RA-Guard implementations are known to be vulnerable to evasion attacks (RFC 7113). The RFC adds a warning for the future: an IPv6-only VPN implementation that does nothing about IPv4 traffic could produce the mirror image of this problem. Operationally, where IPv6-aware clients are unfeasible, an administrator may disable IPv6 connectivity on all interfaces of the host.
sections.plainLanguage: The real fix is a VPN that protects both versions of the protocol. Until then, turning IPv6 off on the computer forces everything through the protected path, though that is a stopgap rather than a cure.

sections.title: The IESG's Objection
sections.content: The RFC is published with an IESG Note that disagrees with how the document frames its own subject. The IESG says the document attributes the leakage problem to VPN software's inability to deal with IPv6, and does not think that is an appropriate characterization. It agrees that when a device supports more than one address family, failing to apply policy to more than one address family is a defect. But it argues that leakage can also occur because of any unencrypted interface allowed on the system, including split tunnels configured in the VPN software itself. While some attacks are unique to an IPv6 interface, the IESG writes, the kind of leakage this document describes is a general problem, not one unique to IPv6-unaware VPN software, and the document does not describe that general issue well enough.
sections.plainLanguage: The body that approved the RFC added a note saying the real problem is broader than IPv6-unaware VPN software: any unprotected path on a computer, including a deliberately split tunnel, can leak traffic, and the document does not fully cover that.
